context: Current closing price of Southern Company (SO): $95.84 USD as of 2026-06-25.
justification_text:
My point estimates across all three horizons were anchored primarily to the current price level, with a slight upward drift built in at longer horizons. The 1-day estimate of 95.9 reflects a near-static expectation that prices rarely move dramatically overnight absent a major catalyst, so the forecast is essentially mean-reverting around the last observed value. The modest increase to 96.1 at one week and 96.5 at one month reflects a small assumed positive drift, likely consistent with either a mildly bullish trend in the underlying asset or a general assumption of slow upward momentum. These increments are deliberately small because I had no strong directional signal suggesting a major move in either direction.

The confidence interval widths expand in a fairly standard way across horizons, reflecting the square-root-of-time scaling that governs uncertainty accumulation in financial or price forecasting. At one day, the 90% CI of roughly plus or minus two points is tight, as there is little time for large deviations to develop. By one week, the interval widens to roughly plus or minus 3.6 points, and by one month it extends to plus or minus seven points, capturing the compounding effect of daily volatility over many trading sessions. These widths were also influenced by the assumed volatility regime at the time of the forecast, which appeared moderate rather than elevated, keeping the intervals from being dramatically wider.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these stated intervals include sudden macroeconomic announcements such as unexpected inflation data, central bank decisions, or geopolitical shocks, any of which could cause a move of five or more points in a single session. On the upside, a strong positive catalyst such as a surprise policy shift or better-than-expected economic data could push prices well above the upper bound of the one-month interval. On the downside, a risk-off event, credit stress, or liquidity shock could easily breach the lower bound. The one-month interval in particular carries meaningful tail risk because it spans enough time for multiple such events to compound, making the stated 103.5 upper and 89.5 lower bounds genuinely possible to breach under stressed conditions.
